إفريقيا ألمانيا أوروبا محاور بيئة ومناخ صحة هجرة ولجوء حقوق الإنسان أبواب سياسة واقتصاد علوم وتكنولوجيا رياضة ثقافة ومجتمع منوعات قضايا راهنة من ألمانيا ملفات من الشرق الأوسط ملفات من شمال إفريقيا ملفات صوتية أحدث الفيديوهات بث مباشر إعلان سياسة السودان مهاجمة شبكات الكهرباء في السودان.. كارثة صحية واقتصادية تلوح في الأفق ندى فاروق 2026/10/30 ٣٠ أكتوبر ٢٠٢٦ تحذيرات من تعطل المستشفيات ومراكز غسيل الكلى وشح المياه في السودان، فيما تتسع تداعيات استهداف البنية التحتية للكهرباء لتشمل الاقتصاد والخدمات الأساسية وسط تصاعد الاتهامات بشأن هجمات المسيّرات. https://p.dw.com/p/5OtAH اجعل DW مصدرك المفضل على Google بعض السودانيين اتجهوا خلال الحرب إلى استخدام بدائل مثل الطاقة الشمسية للتخفيف من آثار الانقطاعات المتكررة صورة من: Ebrahim Hamid/AFP إعلان إلى أي مدى يمكن أن تتحول الهجمات المتكررة على محطات الكهرباء في السودان إلى كارثة صحية تهدد حياة الملايين؟ سؤال يتصاعد مع تزايد التحذيرات من التداعيات الخطيرة لاستهداف البنية التحتية للطاقة، في ظل اعتماد المستشفيات ومراكز غسيل الكلى ووحدات العناية المركزة على الكهرباء لتقديم خدمات طبية حيوية تنقذ الأرواح. وفي وقت يعاني فيه القطاع الصحي من تدهور واسع بسبب الحرب، حذّرت شبكة أطباء السودان من أن استمرار هذه الهجمات يضاعف المخاطر التي تواجه المرضى، ويعمّق معاناة المدنيين، خصوصًا الفئات الأكثر هشاشة التي تعتمد على الرعاية الصحية المستمرة. تصعيد حرب المسيّرات إظلام يطال الشبكة القومية دخلت الأزمة السودانية مرحلة جديدة أكثر خطورة مع تحول الطائرات المسيّرة الانتحارية إلى سلاح رئيسي لشل البنية التحتية، حيث أدت هجمات مكثفة استهدفت محطات التحويل والتوليد الرئيسية في عدة ولايات سودانية إلى إظلام واسع وتوقف شبه كامل للشبكة القومية للكهرباء. وتشير الاتهامات الحكومية والعسكرية إلى مسؤولية قوات الدعم السريع عن إطلاق هذه المسيّرات الانتحارية ومسيّرات (FPV) سريعة التوجيه من منصات تقع في مناطق نفوذها، إلى جانب أنباء عن عبور بعضها بالقرب من الحدود الشرقية، بهدف تعطيل الخدمات الأساسية وضغط المرافق الخدمية في مناطق سيطرة الجيش. وفي المقابل، تواصل قوات الدعم السريع نفيها الاستهداف المباشر للأعيان المدنية، متبادلة الاتهامات مع الجيش السوداني بشأن القصف الجوي والدمار الميداني. من جانبها، قرعت المنظمات الدولية ناقوس الخطر؛ إذ حذر مكتب الأمم المتحدة لتنسيق الشؤون الإنسانية (أوتشا - OCHA) من العواقب الكارثية لاستهداف منشآت الطاقة، مؤكداً أن ذلك ينتهك قواعد القانون الدولي الإنساني. وجاءت التحذيرات متزامنة مع دعوات دولية وخليجية و فرنسا بضرورة التوقف الفوري عن استهداف الأعيان المدنية ووقف تدفق التقنيات العسكرية لطرفي النزاع. وعلى الصعيد الإنساني، دفع القطاع الصحي الفاتورة الأثقل لهذه الضربات، حيث أعلنت تقارير طبية وأممية خروج أكثر من 70% إلى 80% من المرافق الصحية عن الخدمة. وأدى انقطاع التيار وتذبذب إمدادات الوقود المخصصة للمولدات إلى تهديد حياة آلاف المرضى في أقسام العناية المكثفة وحضّانات الأطفال وحديثي الولادة، إلى جانب توقف مراكز غسيل الكلى وتلف كميات كبيرة من اللقاحات والأدوية المخزنة. حذّرت شبكة أطباء السودان من أن استمرار استهداف محطات الكهرباء لا يهدد فقط استقرار الخدمات الأساسية، بل يضع حياة آلاف المرضى على المحك، مع تزايد احتمالات توقف الأجهزة الطبية وتعطل الخدمات العلاجية المنقذة للحياة في مناطق واسعة من البلاد. من يدفع الثمن؟ تقول أسماء (اسم مستعار)، وهي إحدى المقيمات في العاصمة السودانية الخرطوم ، لـ DW عربية، إن أزمة انقطاع الكهرباء ليست المشكلة الوحيدة التي تواجه السكان، موضحة أن نقص الوقود و غاز الطهي ووسائل المواصلات والخبز زاد من صعوبة الحياة اليومية. وأضافت: "ليست المشكلة الكهرباء فقط، بل الوقود وغاز الطبخ والغازولين والمواصلات والخبز. الحياة متوقفة تقريبًا بشكل كامل". وأشارت إلى أن انقطاع الكهرباء يؤثر بشكل مباشر على المرضى الذين يحتاجون إلى حفظ أدويتهم في درجات حرارة مناسبة، قائلة: "نحتفظ ببعض الأدوية التي تحتاج إلى التبريد، لكن ليس الجميع يملك نظام طاقة شمسية، كما أن تكلفته مرتفعة جدًا ولا تسمح الظروف المعيشية لغالبية الناس بشرائه. الوضع صعب للغاية، ويكاد يكون من المستحيل الاستغناء عن الكهرباء". أما حسان، من سكان أم درمان القديمة، فيقول لـ DW عربية إن المنطقة تعيش منذ ثلاثة أيام شبه انقطاع كامل للكهرباء، مشيرًا إلى أن التيار لا يعود إلا لساعات محدودة. وأضاف: "الثلاجات توقفت تمامًا، كما تعطلت مواتير ضخ المياه، ما تسبب في أزمة حقيقية في الحصول على المياه. كذلك تواجه الأفران والمخابز صعوبات كبيرة بسبب انقطاع الكهرباء وشح المياه". وأوضح أن بعض المخابز تمكنت من الحصول على الغازولين، لكن المشكلة الأساسية ما زالت تتمثل في انقطاع الكهرباء وتأثيره على إمدادات المياه والخدمات اليومية. وحذر من تفاقم الأوضاع إذا استمر الوضع على ما هو عليه، قائلًا: "إذا استمر انقطاع الكهرباء، فسيصبح الوضع سيئًا للغاية، لأن كل شيء مرتبط بها، من المياه إلى حفظ الأغذية وتشغيل الخدمات الأساسية". ومع اتساع تأثير الانقطاعات الكهربائية على حياة السكان والخدمات الأساسية، تصاعدت كذلك حدة المواقف الرسمية بشأن الجهات المسؤولة عن استهداف البنية التحتية . وقالت وزارة الخارجية السودانية إن الهجمات الأخيرة على مرافق البنية التحتية المدنية، بما في ذلك محطات الكهرباء والمياه والمستشفيات والمطارات، تسببت في خسائر بشرية وأضرار جسيمة، معتبرة أنها تهدف إلى تعطيل الخدمات الأساسية وزيادة معاناة المدنيين. وبين الاتهامات المتبادلة بشأن المسؤولية عن الهجمات، يلفت خبراء إلى أن الخسائر لا تقتصر على الأضرار المباشرة التي تلحق بمحطات الكهرباء، بل تمتد إلى الاقتصاد السوداني بأكمله. من إدانة المسيّرات إلى اتهام دول إقليمية.. بدوره يرى الخبير الاقتصادي محمد الناير أن استهداف محطات الكهرباء والطاقة يتنافى مع القوانين والأعراف الدولية، باعتبارها مرافق خدمية مدنية مخصصة لتوفير الخدمات الأساسية للمواطنين وليست أهدافًا عسكرية. وأضاف أن مثل هذه الهجمات تستوجب الإدانة لما تسببه من أضرار مباشرة على حياة الناس والاقتصاد. وأوضح أن الكهرباء تمثل المحرك الأساسي لمعظم الأنشطة الاقتصادية في السودان ، سواء في القطاعات الزراعية أو الصناعية أو الخدمية، وبالتالي فإن أي تراجع في الإمداد الكهربائي ينعكس بصورة مباشرة على الإنتاج والخدمات. وأضاف أن بعض المواطنين اتجهوا خلال الحرب إلى استخدام بدائل مثل الطاقة الشمسية للتخفيف من آثار الانقطاعات المتكررة، إلا أن هذه الحلول لا تكفي لتعويض دور الشبكة القومية، خاصة بالنسبة للقطاعات الإنتاجية الكبرى. وأشار إلى أن الأضرار التي لحقت بالبنية التحتية للكهرباء ستؤثر على الاقتصاد السوداني وعلى استقرار الإمداد الكهربائي خلال الفترة المقبلة، لافتًا إلى أن إصلاح المحطات المتضررة أو استبدالها يحتاج إلى وقت وموارد كبيرة. وختم بالقول إن المواطن السوداني يظل المتضرر الأكبر من هذه الهجمات، مؤكدًا أن تأثيرها يمتد إلى مختلف القطاعات الاقتصادية، لكنه أبدى اعتقاده بأن قدرة السودانيين على التكيف والاعتماد على بدائل محلية، خاصة في القطاع الزراعي، قد تسهم في الحد من بعض آثار الأزمة. أزمة تتجاوز الظلام ولا تقتصر المخاوف من تداعيات هذه الهجمات على الداخل السوداني، إذ أثارت التطورات الأخيرة ردود فعل وتحذيرات على المستوى الدولي. وفي الوقت نفسه، أعربت الأمم المتحدة وفرنسا عن قلقهما إزاء تصاعد هجمات الطائرات المسيّرة في أنحاء السودان، محذرتين من آثارها على المدنيين والبنية التحتية الحيوية. وقالت السفارة الفرنسية في السودان إن الغارات الأخيرة أسفرت عن مقتل مئات المدنيين، بينهم أطفال، وأدت إلى تعطيل خدمات أساسية، مؤكدة أن "لا حل عسكرياً للصراع في السودان" وداعية إلى احترام القانون الإنساني الدولي والعمل من أجل وقف دائم لإطلاق النار. وبين التحذيرات الطبية من انهيار الخدمات الصحية، والمخاوف الاقتصادية من تعطل قطاعات الإنتاج، والتصعيد الدبلوماسي المصاحب لتبادل الاتهامات بشأن هجمات المسيّرات، لم تعد أزمة الكهرباء في السودان مجرد مشكلة خدمية. بل باتت مرآة لأزمة أوسع تختلط فيها تداعيات الحرب بالضغوط الإنسانية والاقتصادية، فيما يبقى ملايين السودانيين في مواجهة يومية مع تحديات الحصول على أبسط مقومات الحياة. ندى فاروق ندي فاروق صحفية رسمية سودانية للجزيرة نت أن العاصمة الروسية موسكو شهدت تحركات لاحتواء التوتر بين السودان وتشاد من جهة، وإذابة الجليد بين الخرطوم ونيروبي من جهة أخرى. وأوضحت المصادر السودانية التي طلبت عدم الإفصاح عن هويتها أن الرئيس المصري عبد الفتاح السيسي جمع رئيس مجلس السيادة السوداني عبد الفتاح البرهان والرئيس الكيني ويليام روتو في حضور رئيس المجلس العسكري الانتقالي في مالي آسيمي غويتا على هامش أعمال القمة الروسية الأفريقية في موسكو. قصص مقترحة list of 2 items list 1 of 2 البرهان يقترح على بوتين منطقة اقتصادية بالبحر الأحمر ومواقع لتعدين الذهب list 2 of 2 هجوم بالمسيّرات يستهدف محطة كهرباء شندي بولاية نهر النيل السودانية end of list واعتبرت المصادر اللقاء خطوة إيجابية لإذابة الجليد واحتواء الخلافات بين البلدين، موضحة أنه جاء بعد أيام من لقاء بين رئيس الوزراء السوداني كامل إدريس، والرئيس الكيني في العاصمة الزيمبابوية هراري، على هامش مشاركته في أعمال القمة 25 لرؤساء دول وحكومات السوق المشتركة لوسط وشرق أفريقيا (كوميسا). وحسب المصادر ذاتها، فإن القاهرة سعت لتنقية الأجواء في شرق أفريقيا من أجل تحقيق الاستقرار والتعاون خاصة في ظل الأوضاع الملتهبة التي تشهدها بعض دول المنطقة من القرن الأفريقي شرقا وحتى الساحل الأفريقي غربا. وتتهم الحكومة السودانية كينيا بمساندة قوات الدعم السريع واستقبال قياداتها، واستضافة مؤتمر لتحالف السودان التأسيسي (تأسيس)، الذي يتزعمه قائد القوات محمد حمدان دقلو (حميدتي)، واعتبرت الخرطوم ذلك تدخلا سافرا في شؤونها الداخلية وتهديدا لأمنها القومي. وردت الخرطوم بوقف استيراد الشاي الكيني الذي يُعد من أهم الصادرات الكينية للسودان، مما أثار انتقادات من المعارضة الكينية تجاه تداعيات سياسات حكومتها الخارجية على مصالح اقتصادها ومزارعيه. وفي المقابل، تنفي الحكومة الكينية هذه الاتهامات، مؤكدة أن موقفها يقتصر على السعي لإيجاد تسوية سلمية للأزمة الإنسانية والسياسية في السودان ودعم استقرار المنطقة. البرهان متحدثا أمام القمة الروسية الأفريقية في موسكو (الجزيرة) لقاء سوداني تشادي كما ذكرت المصادر السودانية أن لقاء وزير الخارجية والتعاون الدولي السوداني محيي الدين سالم أحمد، مع نظيره التشادي أحمد كوقوري، في موسكو اتسم بالصراحة والوضوح، وتم التوافق على تسوية الخلافات عبر القنوات الدبلوماسية واستمرار التواصل بينهما. إعلان وأضافت أن الجانبين شددا على ضرورة تهيئة الأجواء والعمل على تجاوز التحديات التي أثرت في مسار علاقاتهما من أجل فتح صفحة جديدة تعيدها إلى سابق عهدها. وكانت الخارجية ذكرت في بيان مقتضب أن الوزيرين ناقشا عددا من القضايا ذات الصلة بالعلاقات الثنائية بين البلدين، مع التأكيد على أهمية التواصل وإجراء اللقاءات بصورة منتظمة بين الجانبين. وتتهم السودان جارتها الغربية بتسهيل مرور الإمدادات العسكرية والأسلحة والعتاد القادم عبر أراضيها ومطاراتها لصالح قوات الدعم السريع، نظرا لتماسّ الحدود الطويلة والرخوة بين البلدين، ورفضت الحكومة التشادية الاتهامات وطالبتها بالاعتذار. بيد أن الحكومة السودانية تمسكت بموقفها مؤكدة أن لديها أدلة تثبت توفير تشاد ممرات لوجستية لإمداد الدعم السريع بالسلاح والعتاد والمرتزقة الأجانب. وتصاعد التوتر بين الجانبي حيث طردت نجامينا في ديسمبر/كانون الأول 2023، 4 دبلوماسيين سودانيين، وردت الخرطوم بطرد 3 دبلوماسيين تشاديين. شروط السلام وأكد البرهان، خلال كلمته أمام القمة الروسية الأفريقية، في موسكو، أن تحقيق السلام في السودان يجب أن يستند إلى إرادة السودانيين وحدهم، بعيدا عن التدخلات والإملاءات الخارجية، مشددا على تمسك الحكومة بمسار الحوار السوداني الذي يفضي إلى انتقال مدني ديمقراطي وانتخابات حرة ونزيهة. ورأى أن السودان يواجه تحديات كبيرة نتيجة الحرب التي تخوضها القوات المسلحة ضد قوات الدعم السريع، متهما الأخيرة بتلقي دعم سياسي ولوجستي من أطراف إقليمية ودولية. وجدد البرهان رغبة الحكومة السودانية في إنهاء الحرب وتحقيق الاستقرار، بشرط أن تضمن أي تسوية الحفاظ على كرامة الدولة وهيبتها ووحدة أراضيها، وأن تستجيب لتطلعات الشعب السوداني. وفيما يتعلق بالمرحلة السياسية المقبلة، كشف البرهان عن توجه حكومته للعمل على تهيئة الظروف اللازمة للانتقال المدني الديمقراطي، عبر حوار سوداني سوداني يتوافق من خلاله السودانيون على أسس مستدامة للاستقرار السياسي. وأوضح أن التصور المطروح يقوم على فترة انتقالية تعقبها انتخابات حرة ونزيهة، تحت مراقبة إقليمية ودولية، بما يتيح الوصول إلى تسوية سياسية تستند إلى إرادة الشعب السوداني. المصدر: الجزيرة aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo إعلان من نحن من نحن اعرض المزيد من نحن الأحكام والشروط Opposition Parties, UN Agencies Sound Alarm Over Security Incidents, Civilian Safety in Ethiopia 3 minute read By Abraham Tekle October 31, 2026 Share Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin Email Telegram Copy URL UN agencies report tens of thousands fled to Kenya Opposition political parties and United Nations agencies have voiced mounting concern over civilian casualties, security incidents, and displacement across parts of Ethiopia, urging immediate measures to protect citizens, investigate reported violations, and ensure accountability amid ongoing regional violence. The Ethiopian Citizens for Social Justice (EZEMA), in a statement issued on October 27, expressed concern that the government has fallen short of its primary obligation to ensure public safety. EZEMA also criticized public media outlets, including the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), for omitting reports of civilian casualties following incidents in the Arsi Zone of the Oromia Region earlier in the month. Detailing multiple security challenges, the party noted that violence in Arsi, alongside recurring inter-communal clashes in the past months in Gambella and Moyale, has led to loss of life, displacement, and property damage. EZEMA called on federal authorities to take proactive steps to prevent further escalations, transparently investigate institutional shortcomings, and hold responsible parties accountable. Furthermore, the party urged human rights organizations to independently examine the incidents and called for greater public media scrutiny regarding the government’s crisis response. Published on 2026-09-02 By The Reporter Magazine What the Old Developmental State Got Wrong Published on 2026-10-02 By Samson Berhane 25-Year Sentences & Retroactive Laws: Controversial Draft Law Sparks Fears of Growing Authoritarianism in Tigray Published on 2026-06-21 By Yared Nigussie Red Sea Rivalries: What a Shifting Geopolitical Landscape Means for Ethiopia and The Horn Published on 2026-08-31 By Yared Nigussie In a statement dated October 26, Enat Party similarly condemned violence, displacement, and targeted attacks affecting Orthodox Tewahedo believers, clergy, and religious institutions. The party appealed to federal and regional authorities to thoroughly investigate the violations, safeguard civilians, and prosecute perpetrators regardless of their official standing or political affiliation. It also encouraged international organizations, diplomatic missions, and human rights monitors to closely follow the situation, cautioning that it is prepared to organize peaceful public demonstrations under the slogan ‘Beka!’ (Enough!) if its demands for security and accountability remains unmet. Echoing these concerns, the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Party (EPRP) issued a statement condemning killings, abductions, and forced displacements in the Arsi Zone, specifically highlighting Shirka and Chole districts. Citing local information, the party reported multiple deaths, injuries, and the alleged abduction of approximately 50 individuals from their homes. The EPRP advocated for an independent international investigation, the safe release of abducted persons, humanitarian assistance for displaced populations, and legal action against those culpable. These developments align with findings from the Ethiopian Human Rights Council (EHRCO), which documented a pattern of killings, injuries, abductions, and displacement across Oromia, Amhara, Gambella, and Benishangul-Gumuz in its annual human rights report covering June 2025 to June 2026. The council reiterated calls for regional and federal authorities to prioritize civilian protection and comprehensive investigations. From The Reporter Magazine From Unwilling Investors to Bidding Wars: Ethiopia’s T-Bill Market Turns on Its Head Published on 2026-09-03 By Mahlet Mehdi Washington Has Sent a Sufficient Signal to PM Abiy on Military Operations: Ex-CIA Analyst Published on 2026-09-28 By Bewket Abebe Behind Ethiopia’s Stalled Iron Ore Mining Published on 2026-08-29 By Bewket Abebe Cities as Engines of Growth and Nation-Building: Reframing Urbanization Discourses in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) Published on 2026-09-14 By Mussie Delelegn Arega (PhD) While accountability for specific incidents remains heavily contested, Oromia Regional Government Communication Bureau Head Hailu Adugna characterized recent violence in the region as an attempt by an armed group referring to itself as ‘Tsmido’ to ignite ethnic and religious strife. Tsimdo refers to armed forces who claims to forge alliance against the government. Hailu expressed deep regret over the loss of lives and material damage resulting from the unrest. Concurrently, reports of active conflict and civilian casualties have emerged from the Amhara and Tigray regions. International media reported that drone strikes hit the Jari No. 2 displacement camp in the South Wollo Zone of the Amhara Region, resulting in a reported death toll including children—alongside numerous injuries requiring hospitalization. In the Tigray Region of Rama town, local residents reported a separate strike affecting a truck transporting sorghum, causing casualties among individuals gathered at the scene. Additional reports from October detailed airstrikes and drone activity in Adwa, Shire, and Sheraro, resulting in civilian deaths and damage to local infrastructure. The impact of the ongoing security challenges has also spilled across international borders. According to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), clashes near the Ethiopian-Kenyan border have prompted thousands to cross into Kenya via Moyale since October 22. Local authorities estimate that up to 50,000 individuals have crossed, with registration and verification efforts ongoing. Many of those fleeing are women and children, finding temporary shelter in local schools, churches, or with host communities. In response, the UNHCR, alongside the International Organization for Migration (IOM), UNICEF, and the World Food Programme, has launched an appeal for USD8.9 million to provide essential humanitarian assistance to up to 50,000 displaced individuals over a three-month period. The IOM indicated that humanitarian partners are actively preparing for further arrivals. Addressing the broader climate of conflict, UN Secretary-General António Guterres emphasized in a public statement that adherence to international law, addressing root causes, and pursuing political settlements remain the only viable pathways to sustainable peace. “Let’s summon the political will to silence the guns, stop the killing, and build a world where peace for all prevails,” he stated. Reports indicate that clashes near the Ethiopian-Kenyan border have led to the displacement of up to 50,000 individuals, prompting a humanitarian response from agencies like the UNHCR. UN Secretary-General António Guterres emphasized the need for adherence to international law and political solutions to achieve lasting peace. The situation remains critical, with calls for accountability and protection of civilians intensifying amidst the ongoing unrest. (158 words)

When a country’s geographic bottleneck is policed by a deeply militarized dictator with no clear economic vision, the resulting friction transcends ordinary bilateral disputes, elevating infrastructure into a primary casus belli. No regional dynamic illustrates this geopolitical chokehold more acutely than the volatile relationship between Ethiopia and Eritrea. For decades, international observers have viewed Ethiopia’s quest for a seaport through a purely commercial lens, equating it as a matter of trade balances, shipping tariffs, and economic optimization. But as the Red Sea rapidly transforms into one of the most volatile, hyper-militarized maritime corridors on the planet, this perspective is dangerously obsolete. For Ethiopia, a nation of over 130 million people, permanent and reliable access to the sea is no longer just an economic aspiration. It is an existential imperative for national security and survival. This assertion makes sense if viewed critically beyond a shallow attempt to reduce the looming danger to a simple expansionist ambition. One must always reconsider the facts on the ground while analyzing the conundrum in the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia, a country that is only 60 kms from the Red sea, is the most populous landlocked country in the world, whose significant portion of the population is youth and in active pursuit of job opportunities. According to recent IMF reports, the country is also home to the fastest growing economy in the entire sub-Saharan Africa. This is not merely a statistical trivia point framed for political purpose; rather it is a profound strategic vulnerability. Every piece of medicine, fuel, and technology that enters the country, and every single product exported to sustain its economy, depends entirely on the political whims and stability of its coastal neighbors. Currently, Ethiopia relies on Djibouti for roughly 95% of its trade, paying upwards between $1.5 to $2 billion annually in port fees. This single door dependency is an economic chokehold. No sovereign state can safely anchor its future on a single corridor that is vulnerable to external influences. For countries like Ethiopia, the highly volatile security situation in its surrounding doubles down the impact, without mentioning the challenges associated with the growing number of military bases in the region. Should political instability or hostile foreign influence freeze the docks of Djibouti, the Ethiopian economy would collapse triggering an internal humanitarian catastrophe of unprecedented scale. This is what makes Ethiopia’s concern undeniably legitimate and fuels its determination to address what it perceives as an existential threat through any means available. Just as a drowning person instinctively tries every possible option to stay afloat. A nation of 130 million people cannot be trapped in a geographic cage at the mercy of volatile, highly militarized autocratic coastal regime. A stable, secure Horn of Africa is impossible if its largest engine of population and economic powerhouse is kept in a state of permanent anxiety and artificial suffocation. Securing a permanent and dependable commercial and naval gateway to the Red Sea is not an empire building ambition or a luxury. For Ethiopia, it is becoming a simple, legitimate right to breath and it is the only way to bring peace and security in the entire Horn. Encirclement, Exclusion, and Ethiopia’s Security Imperative The urgency underpinning Ethiopia’s vulnerability has been sharply accelerated by the growing securitization of the Red Sea. What was once an open global trade route has become an arena for geopolitical chess, dominated by state coalitions and non-state actors from near and afar. Global and regional powers increasingly framing the vital corridor as a critical national security priority rather than just a commercial shipping lane. Driven by the need to safeguard chokepoints like the Bab el Mandab Strait from asymmetric threats, piracy, and regional conflicts, world powers have rapidly expanded their footprint through a dense concentration of military bases along the coastline. Djibouti has become the primary epicenter of this militarization, uniquely hosting overlapping naval facilities for both the United States (Camp Lemonnier) and China, alongside presence from France and Japan. Concurrently, nations like Russia have sought access, while regional actors such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Turkye, and Israel are all vying for influence via port logistics and security pacts along the broader Horn of Africa. While these external militaries provide short-term protection for international shipping, their crowding presence has ultimately transformed the Red Sea into a complex arena of overlapping geopolitical rivalries and proxy vulnerabilities, weakening the prospects for a self-sustaining regional security framework and brutally doubling down on Ethiopia’s unique vulnerability. As if these threats are not enough, Ethiopia is alarmed by a recent development of an architectural web of alliances orchestrated explicitly to isolate it from its own geographic backyard. The creation of the El Alamein Joint Declaration by Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia is not as a routine diplomatic pact, but a deliberate strategy of encirclement. By codifying that Red Sea governance belongs exclusively to coastal states, regional adversaries seek to permanently deny landlocked Ethiopia a seat at the table. Proofing that the danger felt by Ethiopia is eminent beyond perception and this could potentially leave the country to consider every option to break the chokehold before it is too late. The action Ethiopia should take would be determined based on the scale and level of threats the country is faced with, as the end justifies the means. This encirclement is amplified by Egypt’s aggressive forward deployment rhetoric in the region. Driven by tensions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Cairo is trying to weaponize Ethiopia’s landlocked status by forming tight military and logistical alliances with Eritrea and other states bordering Ethiopia. From the Ethiopian perspective, it is quite clear. Hostile foreign militaries are aspiring to setting up base camps right on its borders, holding the keys to the very maritime gates that feed the Ethiopian population. This is a recuring dangerous move. Previously, when multinational coalitions form to protect Red Sea shipping lines from asymmetric threats like piracy and militant groups, Ethiopia is routinely excluded. Addis Ababa is being forced to watch from the sidelines while its primary economic lifeblood is policed by an alliance sympathetic to its rivals. It is profoundly naïve to expect Ethiopia to remain passive while such a perilous scheme is being orchestrated to threaten the lives of its entire population and its very survival. This reality underscores Ethiopia’s existential need to secure a reliable maritime corridor through which it can establish dependable port services and maintain a sovereign naval capability. Such a capability is essential to safeguard its national interests, protect its flag-bearing vessels, and guarantee its unhindered right to innocent passage under international law. Ethiopia has consistently expressed its preference for cooperation and has repeatedly advanced frameworks centered on mutual economic integration, shared prosperity, and regional interdependence. However, while Ethiopia remains committed to peaceful collaboration, coastal states, particularly Eritrea, should recognize that legal technicalities or strategies aimed at regional containment cannot serve as sustainable solutions to a matter that directly concerns the livelihood, security, and future of such burgeoning population. When the survival and long-term interests of the entire nation is at stake, it is unrealistic to expect Ethiopia to remain passive. It will undoubtedly pursue all the necessary strategic measures to secure its legitimate access to the Red Sea and protect its vital national interests. In doing so, it will ensure that its sovereignty, security, and economic future are safeguarded both on land and at sea. In conclusion, Ethiopia’s demand for access to the sea must be understood by its neighbouring countries as a legitimate strategic and economic and security concerns that deserves serious, constructive, and peaceful consideration. Why would Ethiopia’s quest to establish a military base along the Red Sea coast be considered unacceptable when countries from far beyond the region already maintain military bases and enjoy strategic access to the same coastline? Is it just to deny a neighbouring country with vital security and economic interests in the region an opportunity to negotiate such access, while external powers are permitted to establish a military presence there? The issue should not be approached through double standards or geopolitical rivalries, but through constructive dialogue, mutual respect, and negotiated arrangements that uphold the sovereignty of coastal states while addressing Ethiopia’s legitimate interests. IGAD and the African Union must urgently take their leadership responsibilities by facilitating inclusive regional dialogue and developing a practical framework that addresses Ethiopia’s legitimate aspirations while safeguarding the legitimate interests of neighbouring states. External actors outside the Horn of Africa should be discouraged from pursuing their agendas by fostering hostility and division, rather than promoting cooperation, dialogue, and regional stability. The international community, including the United Nations and other influential partners, should also intensify diplomatic engagement and support a negotiated settlement before the situation deteriorates into a dangerous confrontation with far reaching consequences for the Horn of Africa and beyond. The time to act is now: through timely diplomacy, mutual understanding, and political courage, regional leaders and international stakeholders can transform a potential source of conflict into an opportunity for cooperation, shared prosperity, and lasting peace. Failure to act decisively today risks allowing tensions to spiral into a devastating conflict that the region and the wider world can ill afford. What next? Wikimedia Commons A false-color image of the area surrounding the coastal city of Assab and the Red Sea coast, based on satellite imagery data captured on 23 October 2019. The port of Assab and the risk of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war Amgad Fareid Eltayeb last update on 30 Oct 2026 The dispute between Ethiopia and Eritrea over the Red Sea port of Assab now extends well beyond that of a maritime facility or outlet for international trade. It reflects a structural contradiction between two states with a shared history but divided on issues like sovereignty, security, borders, and the state itself. For Ethiopia, Assab embodies its historical loss of direct access to the sea. This is a growing strategic concern, with the country’s population and economy both having expanded. For Eritrea, the port is a key and inseparable part of its sovereignty, won through a long war of independence. Thus, the port mixes economic interests with domestic power struggles, regional alliances, and foreign intervention, particularly in a region already afflicted by weak state institutions and protracted armed conflicts. The modern roots of the crisis lie in Italian colonial expansion in the 19th century. Italian control of Assab began in 1869 through the Rubattino shipping company, which acquired the right to administer the port from local authorities. Administration passed to the Italian state in 1882, and Assab subsequently became part of Italian Eritrea, formally established as a colony in 1890. With the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, this was a time of intensifying European competition for ports and trade routes through the Red Sea. Italy lost control of East Africa in 1941, when Assab and the rest of Eritrea came under British occupation and administration. Following the Second World War, Eritrea’s future administration was debated. On 2 December 1950, the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 390, recommending the establishment of a federation between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The arrangement came into effect in 1952. It recognised Ethiopia’s legitimate need for access to the sea, and granted autonomy to Eritrea (with its own legislative, executive and judicial institutions responsible for internal affairs) within a federation under the sovereignty of the Ethiopian Crown. The resolution did not grant Ethiopia permanent ownership of Assab as a separate sovereign possession, but it went beyond a commercial agreement between two independent states by establishing a federation with sovereign authority at the federal level, defined powers, and Eritrean autonomy. These legal distinctions remain essential to assessing the competing claims surrounding Assab today. Emperor Haile Selassie gradually undermined Eritrea’s autonomous institutions before abolishing the federal system and fully annexing the territory in 1962. A year earlier, Eritrea’s armed struggle for independence had already begun. The Ethiopian Empire fell in the revolution of 1974, and the military regime of Mengistu Haile Mariam reasserted centralised control through force. Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fighters arrive after eight hours of walking in Mekele, the capital of the Tigray region, Ethiopia, on 29 June 2021. Alliances and interests Opposition to his rule fostered cooperation between the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front (EPLF) and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which was waging a parallel campaign to overthrow the regime. Their common struggle contributed to Mengistu’s defeat in 1991, although the alliance concealed a fundamental difference between their political ambitions: the Eritrean movement sought to establish an independent state, while the Tigrayan movement aimed to overthrow the regime and restructure power within Ethiopia. A common enemy had united them, but victory exposed their conflicting visions of statehood. Eritrea gained independence in 1993 following a popular referendum endorsed by Ethiopia’s new government, then led by Meles Zenawi, and it was recognised by the international community. Independence made Ethiopia landlocked, losing its direct access to the Red Sea. Yet this did not disappear overnight. The country continued to use Assab under arrangements agreed with Eritrea, until mounting economic, territorial and political disputes culminated in the 1998–2000 war. This ended with the Algiers Agreement, followed by the boundary commission’s ruling in 2002. Relations between the two countries remained hostile and Ethiopia shifted almost all its maritime trade to Djibouti. Subsequent demographic and economic developments have sharpened the consequences. Ethiopia now has 135 million people, a growing industrial economy, and a thirst for international trade, but with almost all its foreign trade passing through Djibouti, it depends heavily on a single transit route. That dependence creates genuine economic vulnerabilities. Sign up for our Weekly Newsletter Get the best of Majalla, straight to your inbox. Your newsletter subscriptions are subject to Al Majalla privacy policy and terms and conditions . Ethiopia has 135 million people, a growing industrial base, and a thirst for international trade, but almost all trade depends on a single transit route through Djibouti 'Existential necessity' It is not surprising that a country of Ethiopia's size should want to diversify its maritime outlets and secure reliable access to global markets, but however legitimate its economic needs may be, they confer no sovereign entitlement to another country's territory. The right of access to the sea is fundamentally different from the right to a coastline, just as facilitating trade is distinct from redrawing borders. Since October 2023, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has increasingly presented access to the Red Sea as an existential necessity, bound up with the country's future and security. His rhetoric has extended beyond improving commercial transit arrangements to demands for sovereign maritime access and naval capabilities. He invoked history to portray the loss of Ethiopia's coastline as a historical wrong that now needed to be corrected. This rhetoric has coincided with severe domestic crises, particularly in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with local authorities in Somaliland, a coastal region of Somalia that wants to break away. The proposed arrangement envisaged a stretch of coastline and the establishment of a naval facility in exchange for Ethiopian recognition of Somaliland's independence. Somalia's federal government rejected the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty, triggering tensions. Mediation by Türkiye produced the Ankara Declaration in December 2024, which acknowledged the possibility of Ethiopia securing sustainable commercial access to the sea under Somali sovereignty, without granting it a sovereign coastal outlet. In December 2025, Israel (which also wants Red Sea access) became the first UN member state to recognise Somaliland. Ethiopia's attempt to obtain sovereign maritime access through the Somali coast stalled, which brought renewed attention to the port of Assab, which occupies a distinctive place in Ethiopia's political memory. Somaliland President Abdirahman Abdullahi Mohamed during a press conference with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar at the Presidential Palace in Hargeisa, 6 January 2026. Collapsing rapprochement The rapprochement between Ethiopia and Eritrea that began in 2018 was now collapsing. The reconciliation between Addis Ababa and Asmara had developed into a military alliance against the TPLF during the 2020-22 war, but the Pretoria Agreement, which ended that conflict, was subsequently signed without Eritrea's participation, creating a deep rift between the two countries. With no lasting framework for shared economic interests and mutual security guarantees, relations depended on a convergence of interests and calculations regarding domestic adversaries. As the arrangements underpinning Pretoria unravelled, Eritrea developed ties to the TPLF, despite them having fought so bitterly just a few years earlier. In September 2026, large-scale fighting resumed in Tigray. Ethiopian soldiers advanced, capturing Mekelle, the regional capital, before moving towards the Eritrean border. Thus began the latest and most dangerous phase. Addis Ababa and Asmara severed diplomatic relations and accused each other of military interference, support for armed groups, and aggression. Ethiopia invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter to justify measures it said it was taking in self-defence. Eritrea accused Ethiopia of using these claims as a pretext for seizing Assab. Military movements and mounting threats on both sides have now heightened the risk of war. This escalation cannot be understood in isolation. Foreign states have an interest in the Horn of Africa and seek to exploit state weaknesses. Ethiopia maintains close ties with the United Arab Emirates, which has economic and military influence in the ports of the region and across regional supply networks. Israel's recognition of Somaliland also signalled support for Ethiopia's ambitions to secure maritime access there. For Sudan, which has been ravaged by an ongoing civil war, the prospect of fighting between Ethiopia and Eritrea poses a direct threat. The Sudanese Armed Forces are fighting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which now controls the giant Darfur region in western Sudan. The RSF supply network is said to include the UAE, but Abu Dhabi denies it. The International Crisis Group cites reports that RSF forces are stationed in the Benishangul-Gumuz region near the border and launch attacks from there into Sudan's Blue Nile region. Should war break out, the militarisation of the border, the flow of weapons and fighters, and further waves of displacement would compound these dangers, adding to the burden on Sudan. Any Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore draw in overlapping conflicts and foreign actors. The harbour of Port Sudan on the Red Sea on 24 February 2014. It is Sudan's main seaport and source of 90% of its international trade. Dangers of escalation The maritime trade routes around the Horn of Africa are some of the world's busiest and most sensitive, as they intersect with the strategic interests of regional and global powers. Any extension of hostilities towards Eritrea's coastline would increase the risks to ports and shipping, drive up transport and insurance costs, and add more instability in a maritime corridor already suffering the repercussions of the civil war in Yemen. The African Union has a particular responsibility to turn its calls for restraint into urgent diplomatic action. It could reopen communication channels between Addis Ababa and Asmara, establish verifiable arrangements to prevent military clashes along the border, and support the resumption of a political process to address the conflict in Tigray. Regional governments could likewise approach the crisis as a shared threat to stability, rather than an opportunity to alter the balance of power in their favour. Saudi Arabia and Türkiye could help reduce tensions, forge understandings, and safeguard security in the Red Sea, but foreign powers supplying weapons must also commit to ending any military and financial assistance that fuels confrontation. Some call for peace while supplying the means to wage war. There is no inherent legal conflict between Ethiopia's right of access to the sea and Eritrea's sovereignty over its territory. International law recognises the legitimate interests and transit rights of landlocked states, while granting them no right to seize the territory of coastal countries. Respect for borders inherited at independence remains a cornerstone of the African regional order. Together with the prohibition on the use of force enshrined in the UN Charter, this principle places clear limits on territorial claims. A boatman transports visitors along a shore near the old port of Massawa—located 60 kilometers from the Eritrean capital—including civilians arriving from Ethiopia to visit Eritrea's Dahlak Islands. Contractual agreements, joint investments, and reciprocal security arrangements could provide practical solutions to the question of maritime access without reopening disputes over sovereignty. Ethiopia and Eritrea have already demonstrated that Eritrean independence can coexist with Ethiopian use of the port of Assab. Geography did not end that arrangement; it collapsed because political and security understandings between the two countries broke down. Renewing cooperation will require more than another port agreement; it will demand measures to address mutual security concerns, backed by international guarantees. A region at stake Assab represents a test of the future political and security order in the Horn of Africa, with implications far beyond the fate of a port. Ethiopia's need for maritime access is an economic and strategic reality, but turning that need into a claim to sovereignty is no remedy for the underlying economic problem and threatens to ignite a fresh dispute over borders and legitimacy. For Eritrea, defending independence and sovereignty is compatible with establishing good economic relations with its larger neighbour. For the countries of the Horn of Africa, not least Sudan, preventing war is essential to protecting their own security and sovereignty. In a region exhausted by conflict and the collapse of state institutions, the greatest danger is that an attempt to change Ethiopia's landlocked status by force ignites another war, at a cost to all concerned far greater than any benefit its proponents hope to gain. + / - SAVE SHARE Related topics Tigray Ethiopia Eritrea Red Sea Port international trade Horn of Africa Sudan Related Articles The leaders of Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea met in Alamein Egypt on 4 October to discuss regional tensions. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia has received its first 12 Su-35 fighter jets and is set to acquire four S-400 air defense system batteries, as announced by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. This delivery marks a significant advancement in Ethiopia's national defense capabilities, aimed at enhancing security and deterring potential threats. In a social media statement, PM Abiy highlighted that this achievement is part of Ethiopia's broader strategy to ensure peace and security sustainably. He expressed gratitude to Russian President Vladimir Putin for expediting the delivery ahead of schedule. The acquisition positions Ethiopia as a leader in military modernization within Sub-Saharan Africa, reinforcing its sovereignty and defense capabilities. The announcement coincides with PM Abiy's visit to Moscow for the Third Russia–Africa Summit, which aims to strengthen Ethiopia's ties with Russia and other African nations. This development is seen as a crucial step in bolstering Ethiopia's collective security and long-term national objectives. (159 words)

The latest alert seems to confirm that there is still fighting in the Tigray region of Ethiopia although the regional capital Mekelle is not experiencing active fighting. In an interview with Anchor Media on Thursday, the TPLF spokesperson Dr. Abraham Hagos stated that the organization has finalized preparation for counter-offensive and is reorganized for combat in five fronts. The statement from the Embassy on Wednesday this week stated “Fighting in Tigray appears to be concentrated in areas outside Mekelle and near the border with Eritrea.” It noted that Ethiopian Airlines flights to Shire and Axum, in the Tigray region remain suspended. As was the case with the travel advisory at the beginning of this month, the U.S. Embassy advised citizens to reconsider travelling to Ethiopia and avoid traveling to Afar, Amhara and Tigray regions of Ethiopia. It also advised citizens who are already in those areas to leave if safe to do so. Also, the embassy highlighted the security situation in Moyale, a border town between Ethiopia and Kenya where there had been intense conflict earlier this week. It stated that ” The embassy also continues to monitor ongoing fighting in Moyale, the primary border with Kenya, shared by both the Oromia and Somali regions, which appears to have calmed.” However, it warned that the situation “may change at any time.” Among the actions the embassy recommended to citizens is to avoid “military installations.” Earlier this month, the U.S. disclosed military attacks targeting the capital Addis Ababa as local sources were reporting a drone attack targeting Defense Force Headquarters in the capital Addis Ababa – which Ethiopia did not confirm. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio linked the attacks to what he described as “separatists.” Notably, seven armed groups operating in the different parts of the country formed a coalition in September. It was within less than three weeks after the announcement of the coalition that the Ethiopian Defense Force launched its military operation in the Tigray region. Tigray People’s Liberation Front ( TPLF ) fighters withdrew from many towns in the region including Mekelle which they describe as “strategic retreat” However, media outlets affiliated with the government claim that the TPLF was militarily defeated and is now waging a guerilla war across Northern Tigray. On Friday, Samora Yenus, former defense chief and TPLF member, stated that the TPLF was defeated. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: U.S. Customs Releases Ethiopia-Made Solar Cell Shipments After Supply Chain Review - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: U.S. Customs Releases Ethiopia-Made Solar Cell Shipments After Supply Chain Review 30 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has released shipments of solar cells manufactured at a Japanese company's facility in Ethiopia following a review of its supply chain documentation, SolarQuarter reported. TOYO Co., Ltd., a Japan-headquartered solar manufacturing company, announced on 29 October that CBP had completed its review after the company submitted documentation demonstrating the traceability of its supply chain, including the origins of polysilicon and wafers used in manufacturing the solar cells. The company said it cooperated with US authorities throughout the review process and provided detailed documentation on the sourcing of its production materials. The release of the shipments comes as TOYO seeks to expand its international manufacturing operations and strengthen its presence in the US market. The company operates a manufacturing facility in Humble, Texas, and is pursuing certification under CBP's Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism (CTPAT) programme, which is designed to strengthen supply chain security and import compliance. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn TOYO Chief Executive Officer Takahiko Onozuka welcomed the completion of the review, expressing appreciation for what he described as CBP's professional approach. He said the company remained committed to transparency and regulatory compliance as it expands its US operations. Onozuka also stressed the importance of providing customers with confidence in the origins of solar products through greater supply chain traceability. The development highlights the importance of supply chain documentation and regulatory compliance for solar manufacturers operating across multiple countries, particularly as scrutiny of the origins of imported products increases. The release of the shipments follows an ongoing US investigation into whether solar cell manufacturers operating in Ethiopia are circumventing existing American trade duties on Chinese solar products. In July 2026, Addis Standard reported that the US Department of Commerce had launched a country-wide investigation into imports of silicon solar cells from Ethiopia to determine whether they were circumventing longstanding antidumping and countervailing duty (AD/CVD) orders on Chinese solar products. The investigation followed a petition filed in May 2026 by eight US solar manufacturers -- DYCM Power, First Solar, Qcells, Silfab, Solx, Suniva, Swift Solar and Talon PV -- alleging that two manufacturers operating in Ethiopia, TOYO and Origin Solar, were using Chinese-origin wafers to produce solar cells in Ethiopia before assembling them into solar modules locally or in Vietnam for export to the US. According to the petition, nearly 70% of finished solar modules exported from Ethiopia contained Chinese components and underwent processing allegedly covered by existing US trade restrictions. Solar Power World reported that imports of Ethiopia-origin solar cells and modules, which were virtually nonexistent before July 2025, reached an estimated $277 million in the second half of that year, with shipments continuing to increase in 2026. The petitioners argued that the surge in exports coincided with increased shipments of key solar manufacturing inputs from China to Ethiopia. Both TOYO and Origin Solar subsequently submitted factual information to the Department of Commerce in response to the allegations. The investigation is expected to reach a preliminary determination by 10 December 2026, with a final decision anticipated around 10 May 2027. In the meantime, US Customs and Border Protection was instructed to suspend liquidation of relevant imports and apply cash deposit requirements pending the outcome. Any duties imposed could be applied retroactively to the investigation's initiation date. "Since Ethiopia's return to a sea port is inevitable, working closely and through dialogue with regional countries is essential," Kindu said on Friday, a day after the conclusion of a regional maritime security forum organized by the Ethiopian Navy Headquarters, according to the army. The forum brought together naval commanders and representatives from Yemen, Oman, Djibouti, Somaliland, and Puntland to exchange experiences and explore joint approaches to maritime search and rescue operations and regional security challenges. ENDF said the forum was organized with the support of the European Union. Kindu described the gathering as "the first of its kind in Ethiopia" to discuss regional maritime search and rescue plans, saying it demonstrated the Ethiopian Navy's growing capabilities and readiness to engage in regional and continental maritime affairs. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He also highlighted growing security challenges around the Strait of Hormuz, warning that threats in the area could increasingly affect the wider region. No country, regardless of its strength, could independently ensure maritime security or resolve emerging challenges, he said, emphasizing the need for countries of different sizes to pool their capabilities. "The participating countries of the forum must work together to solve the problems observed in the region," Kindu said, adding that regional cooperation was essential to addressing maritime threats and ensuring safe maritime movement. Ethiopian Navy Deputy Commander for Operations Commodore Jemal Tufisa said the forum had helped establish practical foundations for regional cooperation through cross-border information sharing, identifying areas of concern, and conducting joint operational exercises. "We trust that upon returning to your respective countries, you will translate the lessons gained from the workshop into action, working effectively on regional maritime security and performing tasks with international acceptance," Jemal said. Rear Admiral Kenneth Nyagah, a search and rescue project expert, and Master Kuraja Mishini, manager of the Djibouti Code of Conduct, commended the Ethiopian Navy's initiative in creating communication channels for information sharing, coordinated decision-making, and joint responses to regional threats. Both expressed their commitment to continued cooperation. Facebook Twitter Print Email Somalia looks to the future as the UN's political mission closes By Daniel Dickinson 31 October 2026 Peace and Security “The story of the UN's political engagement in Somalia has been one of persistence, partnership and adaptation,” Raisedon Zenenga , the UN Secretary-General's Deputy Special Representative for Somalia has said, as three decades of UN political missions in the Horn of Africa country comes to an end on 31 October. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia, known as UNTMIS , wraps up its work on Saturday and according to Mr. Zenenga “ while significant challenges remain, the closure of UNTMIS comes after considerable progress by Somalia since the early years of international efforts to support the country's recovery .” Somalia has undergone a profound transformation since the early 1990s, when the collapse of central State institutions and the outbreak of civil war ushered in years of conflict, instability and humanitarian crises. UN Somalia/Adihamiid Mohamed Raisedon Zenenga, Officer-in-Charge of UNTMIS, delivers remarks at a ceremony marking the closure of the mission. The conflict sparked a major outflow of refugees and internal displacements, while ongoing insecurity, contested electoral processes and constitutional reform, as well as recurrent climatic shocks – including droughts and floods – compounded humanitarian needs and presented formidable challenges to the country's recovery. Somalia’s responsibility Successive political missions accompanied Somalia through critical stages of its peacebuilding and State-building journey, supporting Somali-led efforts to restore governance, rebuild institutions and foster national reconciliation. With the end of the UNTMIS, it is now Somali institutions which will take on the full responsibility for the country’s recovery with support from UN agencies already working in the country. “Somalia today possesses national and federal institutions that did not exist when the UN’s political engagement began. Progress has been made in State formation, political inclusion, constitutional processes, human rights frameworks and the development of governance structures that enable Somali-led decision-making ,” said Mr. Zenenga. “However, continued engagement by the international community will remain important to sustaining progress and addressing outstanding priorities,” he added. © WFP/Arete/Ahmed Luzako A member of staff of the World Food Programme (left) talks to a woman in a camp for people who were forced to flee their homes. Humanitarian and development support That engagement includes some 25 UN entities that are still working across Somalia on humanitarian and development support. In September, in the town of Balcad, a run-down vegetable market got a makeover from the UN's migration agency, IOM . Tweet URL There are now 56 sturdy stalls, running water and solar lighting. About 70 per cent of the stalls went to women-headed households, women-led businesses and small enterprises. Elsewhere, Somalia's health ministry, working with UNICEF , launched national guidelines on caring for newborns, including babies who are small or sick. In Puntland, where nearly a million children are out of school, the UN's food agency FAO is backing a school meals programme that links 1,330 local farmers and fisherfolk to schools serving 18,700 children, so kids eat and families earn. And in Baidoa, mine action experts from UNMAS helped Somali authorities teach hundreds of students and teachers how to spot explosive dangers. A complex crisis The UN's humanitarian affairs office, OCHA , calls the situation in Somalia one of the world's most complex crises. Conflict and climate shocks keep feeding each other, and families who fled drought or fighting have often been uprooted a second or third time by floods or fresh violence. This year, 4.8 million Somalis, out of a population of just under 20 million, need humanitarian help . Aid agencies are asking for $852 million to reach 2.4 million people, just half of those in need, and by mid-October only about 35 per cent of that had arrived. The UN Secretary-General also wants continued support to tackle the threat from the terror group Al-Shabaab and to help Somalia move to a gradual, sustainable security transition. © WFP/Arete/Abdirahman Yussuf Mohamud Children are ferried across flood water in a plastic barrel in Hirshabelle State, Somalia. Looking ahead, one huge challenge for Somalia's leaders after October is poverty. They'll need to tackle it while steadying an economy that's still fragile. It leans heavily on subsistence farming, livestock, money sent home by relatives abroad and pastoralism. The country imports more than 90 per cent of its essential goods , according to OCHA . UN will remain While UNTMIS is closing down, the United Nations is not leaving . UN humanitarian and development agencies continue to support Somalia and its people. “Today is not an end to the partnership between the United Nations and Somalia,” Deputy Special Representative Zenenga said. "It marks the conclusion of one chapter and the beginning of another.” ♦ Receive daily updates directly in your inbox - Subscribe here to a topic. ♦ Download the UN News app for your iOS or Android devices. somalia.summary: The UN's political mission in Somalia, known as UNTMIS, officially concludes on October 31, marking the end of three decades of international engagement aimed at stabilizing the country. Raisedon Zenenga, the UN Secretary-General's Deputy Special Representative for Somalia, highlighted the mission's role in supporting Somalia's recovery from civil war and state collapse in the early 1990s. Despite significant progress in governance and institutional development, Somalia faces ongoing challenges, including humanitarian crises exacerbated by conflict and climate shocks. With the mission's closure, Somali institutions will assume full responsibility for the country's recovery, supported by various UN agencies still active in the region. The UN continues to emphasize the importance of international support to address pressing issues such as poverty and security threats from groups like Al-Shabaab. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers,” Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, chief of Uganda’s defense forces, wrote on X. advertisements Ugandan authorities have not publicly announced how many troops are leaving, which bases will be handed over first or when the withdrawal will be completed. Uganda remains the largest troop contributor to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, or AUSSOM. The African Union authorized 4,500 Ugandan troops for the mission, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia at the start of 2025. AUSSOM’s mandate includes supporting Somali forces against al-Shabab, protecting civilians and key infrastructure, and gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somali security institutions. The mission’s current transition plan envisages a phased drawdown toward a final exit by December 2029, subject to security conditions. Uganda first deployed troops to Somalia in March 2007 as the lead contingent in the African Union Mission in Somalia, or AMISOM, becoming one of the longest-serving foreign military contributors to the country’s security operations. Ugandan forces have since fought in some of the most significant battles against al-Shabab and have operated across Mogadishu and large parts of Lower Shabelle. The deployment has also come at a heavy cost. Ugandan troops have suffered repeated casualties in al-Shabab attacks, including major assaults on African Union bases over the course of the mission. The announcement comes as AUSSOM faces persistent funding shortages. The African Union Peace and Security Council has repeatedly warned that inadequate and unpredictable financing threatens the mission’s operations and has called for additional international support. The AU has also emphasized that decisions over AUSSOM’s future and troop withdrawals should be based on assessments of conditions on the ground and coordinated with Somalia to avoid creating security gaps. Uganda has remained a central part of that security architecture. Earlier this year, the African Union praised Kampala for deploying additional troops to Somalia on a bilateral basis as a temporary response to deteriorating security conditions. Al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, continues to control or operate across parts of rural southern and central Somalia despite nearly two decades of military pressure from Somali forces and their international partners. Kainerugaba’s announcement therefore represents a significant shift in Uganda’s long-running role in Somalia, but it remains unclear whether the move marks the beginning of a full national withdrawal or a phased reduction coordinated with AUSSOM and Somali authorities. The decision was announced in an official notice published in the U.S. Federal Register on October 27, 2026, following a Coast Guard assessment of security arrangements at Somalia's ports. advertisements The Coast Guard determined that Somalia is not currently maintaining effective measures to prevent acts of terrorism at its port facilities. As a result, vessels arriving in the United States from Somali ports will be subject to additional security and port entry requirements. The measures were introduced under powers granted by the Maritime Transportation Security Act and other federal laws governing maritime and port security. Somalia is now among 24 countries identified by the United States as failing to maintain effective counterterrorism measures at their ports. Others on the list include Iran, Iraq, Libya, Sudan, Syria, Yemen, Venezuela and North Korea. According to the Federal Register notice, the decision took effect on October 27, 2026. The notice was signed by Admiral Nathan A. Moore, the Coast Guard's Deputy Commandant for Operations. The designation means vessels arriving from Somali ports will face additional security procedures when entering U.S. waters. However, the notice does not detail all the specific measures that affected vessels will be required to follow. Posted by: Horseed Staff Hawlgalka siyaasadeed ee Qaramada Midoobay ee Soomaaliya (UNTMIS) ayaa maanta oo Sabti ah, 31-ka October 2026,… 31 October, 2026 Share Tweet Hawlgalka siyaasadeed ee Qaramada Midoobay ee Soomaaliya (UNTMIS) ayaa maanta oo Sabti ah, 31-ka October 2026, si rasmi ah u soo gabagabeynaya shaqadiisa, kaddib markii uu dhammaaday muddadii labada sano ahayd ee loogu talagalay kala-guurka iyo wareejinta waajibaadkii uu hayay, inkastoo aysan tallaabadaasi soo afmeeri doonin shaqooyinka Qaramada Midoobey ee Soomaaliya. Xafiiskaan ayaa la aasaasay 30-kii October 2024, kaddib markii Golaha Ammaanka ee Qaramada Midoobay uu ansixiyey qaraarka tirsigiisu yahay 2753, waxaana uu shaqada si rasmi ah u bilaabay 1-dii November 2024, isagoo beddeley UNSOM (United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia) oo la aasaasay 3-dii June 2013, kaas oo muddo ka badan 11 sano ka shaqeynayay taageerada siyaasadeed, dib-u-dhiska dowladnimada iyo nabadeynta Soomaaliya. UNTMIS ayaa waajibaadkiisu ahaa taageerada dhismaha dowladnimada, dib-u-eegista dastuurka, dadaallada doorashooyinka xor iyo xalaasha ah, dib-u-heshiisiinta siyaasadeed, ilaalinta xuquuqda aadanaha, horumarinta sharciga iyo garsoorka, taageerada hay’adaha amniga iyo isku-duwidda taageerada deeq-bixiyeyaasha caalamiga ah. Xiritaanka UNTMIS ayaa qayb ka ah qorshe kala-guur oo ay si wadajir ah u diyaariyeen Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya iyo Qaramada Midoobay, kaas oo ujeeddadiisu ahayd in mas’uuliyadaha hawlgalka si tartiib-tartiib ah loogu wareejiyo hay’adaha dowladda Soomaaliya, xafiiska isku-duwidda Qaramada Midoobay ee dalka iyo hay’adaha kale ee ay khuseyso, iyadoo ujeedadu tahay in Soomaaliya ay xilligaan dareento lahaanshaha mas’uuliyadda nabad-dhisidda iyo dowlad-dhisidda. Dhanka amniga, ciidamada Midowga Afrika ee ku sugan Soomaaliya ayaa lagu bilaabay qorshe dib-u-habayn iyo dhimista joogitaankooda, iyadoo mas’uuliyadda amniga si tartiib ah loogu wareejinayo ciidamada dowladda Soomaaliya, iyadoo Ciidamada Uganda oo ahaa kuwii ugu horreeyey ee magaca AMISOM ku yimaada Soomaaliya 2007 gacantana ku hayey xafiisayda dowladda, garoomada, dekedo iyo goobo muhiim ah ay bilaabeen in qaybo kamid ah dib loogu celiyo dalkooda. Hirgelinta go’aankaan ayaa yimid kadib markii 29-kii October 2026, uu Taliyaha Ciidanka Difaaca Uganda, Jeneraal Muhoozi Kainerugaba, shaaciyey in ciidamadooda ay bilaabeen inay Soomaaliya ka baxaan, kaddib ku dhowaad 20 sano oo ay dalka ka howlgaleen, iyadoo maalintii xigtay oo ahayd 30-ka October, ay Muqdisho ka ambabexeen ciidankii ugu horreeyey oo ka kooban 109 askari oo Uganda ah, sida ay baahiyeen warbaahinta Uganda. Uganda ayaa muddo dheer ahayd dalka ugu badan ee ciidamada ka geeya hawlgallada Midowga Afrika ee Soomaaliya, waxaana ciidamadeedu ka qaybqaateen howlgalladii AMISOM, ATMIS iyo AUSSOM, iyadoo bixitaankooda loo sababeeyey dhaqaale yarida soo wajahdey hawlgalka kadib markii la waayey dhaqaalihii caalamku ku taageeri jirey sugidda ammaanka Soomaaliya. The meeting focused on security arrangements in Baidoa and efforts to prevent attacks by fighters aligned with Laftagareen, according to reports about the discussions. The talks come as Madobe faces growing pressure to defend his administration amid renewed clashes and reports of advances by forces loyal to the former regional leader in parts of the Bay region. Madobe assumed control of the South West State administration in March after Somali federal forces seized Baidoa, forcing Laftagareen to leave office and flee the city. The takeover followed a political dispute between Laftagareen and the federal government over the region’s leadership and constitutional changes. Ethiopian troops have maintained a presence in parts of South West State as part of international security efforts in Somalia. Their position has become a sensitive issue as the political confrontation between the two Somali camps has increasingly turned into an armed struggle. Reports say Ethiopian commanders have declined to take sides in the dispute, maintaining that their responsibility is to support security operations against al-Shabab rather than become involved in a political conflict between Somali factions. The reported refusal presents a challenge for Madobe’s administration as it seeks to strengthen its security position in and around Baidoa. A separate report by Shabelle Media Network said Madobe met with the commander of the African Union peacekeeping force’s Third Sector on Oct. 30. That meeting was publicly described as focusing on security cooperation and operations against al-Shabab. The latest developments underscore the difficulties facing the South West administration as it seeks to consolidate its authority while confronting armed opposition from Laftagareen’s supporters. Whatever occurs between the two countries is a matter for them alone; we are not a part of it, and there are no conflicts in which we seek to intervene,” the president said. Hassan Sheikh emphasized that Somalia's foreign policy is guided by peaceful coexistence, mutual understanding and cooperation with neighboring countries. He said the government's priority was to maintain stability at home while fostering constructive relations with other countries. The president described Somalia's guiding principle as being at peace with itself and with the rest of the world, stressing that Mogadishu does not seek involvement in conflicts between other nations. His remarks come amid renewed diplomatic and political tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, raising concerns about the potential consequences for security and stability across the Horn of Africa. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated amid disagreements over regional security and competing political interests. Somalia maintains diplomatic relations with both countries and has emphasized the importance of dialogue and cooperation in addressing regional disputes. Hassan Sheikh's latest remarks reinforce Mogadishu's stated position of avoiding involvement in the Ethiopia-Eritrea dispute while maintaining working relationships with both governments. “Somalia would continue prioritizing peaceful relations and cooperation as part of broader efforts to promote stability in the Horn of Africa,” he added. مدربه جوزيف زينباور، بعد أن استوفى عقوبة الإيقاف لمباراة واحدة عقب طرده في الجولة الأولى. حيث يخطط المدرب لاتخاذ خطوات حاسمة، قبل بدء مشوار الفريق في دور المجموعات من مسابقة دوري أبطال أفريقيا . زينباور يوسع دائرة خياراته مع الهلال كشفت مصادر موثوقة لموقع winwin، أن زينباور سيتخذ خطوة جادة بتوسيع دائرة اختياراته في الفترة المقبلة، بحثًا عن مواجهة ضغط جدول مباريات الدوري الرواندي؛ وذلك بعد أن سبق له استبعاد عدد من اللاعبين وألحقهم بالفريق الرديف، الذي يخوض مباريات ودية قوية. اقرأ أيضًا الهلال السوداني يصدم جماهيره بخسارة قاسية في الدوري الرواندي كمال: نحترم بيراميدز ولا نخشاه.. والهلال قادر على المنافسة ويسعى المدرب من خلال هذه الخطوة، إلى تحديد قائمته المثالية للمشاركة في دوري أبطال أفريقيا، علما بأنه سيتم تأجيل عدد من مباريات الفريق في الدوري الرواندي خلال تلك الفترة. ويستهل رفاق
